data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The night-time urban heat island is primarily an evapotranspiration deficit: impervious urban surfaces lack vegetation and soil moisture, so daytime sensible heat storage is not dissipated as latent heat, leaving more heat to be released nocturnally; the gap is larger in cities with less irrigation and green space.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If nocturnal UHI magnitude is uncorrelated with green space fraction or irrigation intensity across cities, the evapotranspiration deficit mechanism fails.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If arid cities with minimal vegetation show smaller nocturnal UHI than humid, vegetated cities, the mechanism may be secondary.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If daytime urban-rural humidity gradients do not track the nocturnal temperature gap, the latent heat explanation is weakened.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"In vegetated countryside, evapotranspiration converts incoming radiation into latent heat throughout the day, limiting sensible heat storage. In the city, impervious surfaces prevent this latent heat flux, so excess energy is stored as sensible heat in thermal mass and released after sunset. The nocturnal temperature gap thus depends on vegetation and irrigation: cities with more green space experience weaker nocturnal UHI because daytime evapotranspiration reduces the heat available for nighttime release.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
